questions.prompt: `docker stop` takes exactly ten seconds on a container whose only process is `sleep 600`. Why?
choices: sleep ignores SIGTERM on every system, so Docker always has to wait out the grace period and then send SIGKILL
Docker waits a fixed ten seconds on every stop so the process can flush buffers, even when it exits at once
The sleep binary is not installed in the image, so Docker cannot signal it and must wait for the timeout
As PID 1, sleep gets no default SIGTERM action, so the signal is ignored until Docker sends SIGKILL
questions.explanation: The kernel does not apply default signal actions to PID 1. A process that would die from SIGTERM anywhere else ignores it as PID 1 unless it installs a handler, which is why init systems and tini exist.

questions.prompt: What is a zombie process and why does PID 1 have to care?
choices: An exited process whose status was never collected with wait(); orphans go to PID 1, which must reap them
A process hung in uninterruptible I/O (D state) that cannot be killed, which PID 1 must forcibly terminate
A process whose parent has exited and that keeps running, which PID 1 must stop because it has no owner
A process started with nohup that ignores SIGHUP, which PID 1 must clean up when the terminal session closes
questions.explanation: Every exited child stays in the process table until its parent calls wait(). Orphaned processes are adopted by PID 1, so a PID 1 that never reaps leaks process-table entries forever.

questions.prompt: Why does the supervisor use `waitpid(-1, WNOHANG)` in a loop instead of one blocking `wait()` per SIGCHLD?
choices: A blocking wait() is deprecated on Linux, and waitpid is the only call the kernel still supports for reaping children
WNOHANG makes each reap faster, so one waitpid call per SIGCHLD is enough to keep up with a busy supervisor
Signals coalesce: several children can exit under one pending SIGCHLD, so reap in a loop until none are left
It lets the supervisor avoid signals completely, because polling waitpid replaces the SIGCHLD handler in full
questions.explanation: SIGCHLD is not queued per child. One delivery may stand for many exits; a single wait would leave the others as zombies.

questions.prompt: An ENTRYPOINT script ends with `node server.js`. Pressing Ctrl-C does nothing and `docker stop` waits ten seconds. What is the one-word fix?
choices: sudo
exec
nohup
setsid
questions.explanation: Without exec, the shell is PID 1 and node is its child; the shell ignores SIGTERM and does not forward it. `exec node server.js` replaces the shell so node becomes PID 1 with its own handler.

questions.prompt: In the supervisor, why does begin_shutdown() clear the pending restarts before forwarding the signal?
choices: A child killed by the forwarded SIGTERM looks like a failure, so on-failure would restart it mid-shutdown
Pending restarts hold memory that the supervisor must free before it can forward any signal to its children
Pending restarts become invalid after any signal arrives, so they cannot be run later without a full reset
It does not; restarts keep running during shutdown so services stay available until the grace period ends
questions.explanation: A SIGTERM-terminated child looks like a failure to the restart policy. Shutdown must win; systemd and Kubernetes encode the same rule as a stopping state during which restart policies are suspended.

questions.prompt: Kubernetes sends SIGTERM, waits terminationGracePeriodSeconds, then SIGKILLs. Which lesson concept is that?
choices: Backoff, where each retry waits longer and the pod field sets how long the delay may grow before giving up
Zombie reaping, where the kubelet collects the exit status of each container before it sends the SIGKILL
The same forward-then-escalate shutdown you built, with the grace period exposed as a pod field
The exec form of ENTRYPOINT, where Kubernetes runs the process directly so it receives SIGTERM first
questions.explanation: Graceful shutdown is forward SIGTERM, wait a bounded time, escalate to SIGKILL. The pod field, docker stop -t and the supervisor's --grace are the same knob at three layers.
